description_full: REX American Resources Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, produces and sells ethanol in the United States. The company provides corn, distillers grains, ethanol, distillers corn oil, gasoline, and natural gas. It also offers dry distillers grains with soluble, which is used as a protein in animal feed. REX American Resources Corporation was formerly known as REX Stores Corporation and changed its name to REX American Resources Corporation in June 2010. The company was founded in 1980 and is headquartered in Dayton, Ohio.

financial_summary: REX American Resources Corporat is a small-cap basic materials business with a $1.3B market cap on $650M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +20% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 10% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $49M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 75× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

sect: The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 39% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 26% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.68, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.43 vs 5y 0.51), so read it loosely.
About $9.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 56% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 72% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $30.75 (margin of safety -28%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 8%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $26.18 to $37.61 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 10.8 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.8% (below the risk-free rate).
The price implies 10.9% annual cash-flow growth, 6pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 8% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.85).
It runs a 10% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.42x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $358.0M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 20.4% over 3 years, 11.8% over 5 years and 4.1% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 42%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 7.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 4.5x depreciation (10.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 54.0% on average.
own: Insiders own 13.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 84%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $7.1M sold).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (2.6% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 132 employees, each generates about $4.9M of revenue, 7.7x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 3.4% a year.
That works out to $374K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.0M (1x revenue per employee).
